stats.line: About 1 in 5 people who ever use cocaine become dependent at some point. Half of them get there within about 4 years.
stats.mirror: Guys who only do lines on nights out and think they're safe.

basis.design: national survey, same people interviewed twice (NESARC)
basis.who: US adults who had ever used cocaine
basis.measured: estimated lifetime chance of going from first use to the older DSM-IV criteria for dependence

stats.caveat: A lifetime estimate from people's memory. It uses the strict older definition. The other 4 in 5 never reached it, but may still have had problems.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Pérez de los Cobos J, Hasin DS, et al. (2011). Probability and predictors of transition from first use to dependence on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis, and cocaine: results of NESARC. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.
ref.quote: The cumulative probability estimate of transition to dependence was 67.5% for nicotine users, 22.7% for alcohol users, 20.9% for cocaine users, and 8.9% for cannabis users.

stats.line: Using weekly meant about 2× the odds of cocaine addiction about 3 years later; 1–3 times a month, 1.7×, versus less than monthly.
stats.mirror: Weekend users who think 'a few times a month' can't hook them.

basis.who: US adults who had ever used cocaine
basis.measured: how often people had used cocaine at their heaviest, and whether they had cocaine use disorder at the second interview

stats.caveat: Odds, not risk. The comparison group (less than monthly) is not risk-free. Self-reported. It does not say what share of weekly users got hooked.

ref.cite: Aharonovich E, Scodes J, Wall MM, et al. (2021). The relationship of frequency of cocaine use to substance and psychiatric disorders in the U.S. general population. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.
ref.quote: use ≥1x/week and use 1-3 times a month was associated with cocaine use disorder in 2004-2005 (aOR = 2.13 and aOR = 1.67, respectively).

stats.line: About 2 in 100 American adults used cocaine in the past year (2018–19). Users were more often men aged 18–49.
stats.mirror: Guys who feel cocaine is everywhere in their circle.

basis.n: yearly national samples (size not given in the abstract)
basis.measured: self-reported cocaine use in the past 12 months, and cocaine use disorder

stats.caveat: Far fewer adults, 0.37%, met the criteria for cocaine use disorder. Self-reported. Your city or friend group can be very different.

ref.cite: Mustaquim D, Jones CM, Compton WM (2021). Trends and correlates of cocaine use among adults in the United States, 2006–2019. Addictive Behaviors.
ref.quote: The annual average estimated prevalence of past-year cocaine use among adults was highest in 2006-2007 (2.51%), declined to 1.72% in 2010-2011, and then increased to 2.14% in 2018-2019.

stats.line: Of new cocaine users, about 5–6% were already hooked within 2 years of first use. Smoking crack or injecting made it more likely.
stats.mirror: Men in their first year or two of 'just partying'.

basis.design: national household survey (NHSDA, now called NSDUH)
basis.n: 114,241 surveyed; 1,081 had first used cocaine in the past 24 months
basis.measured: share of recent first-time users who had met dependence criteria since they started

stats.caveat: Covers only the first 2 years; the risk keeps building after that. Self-reported. Young adults aged 21–25 had lower early risk here.

ref.cite: O'Brien MS, Anthony JC (2005). Risk of becoming cocaine dependent: epidemiological estimates for the United States, 2000–2001. Neuropsychopharmacology.
ref.quote: Between 5 and 6% of these recent-onset users had become cocaine dependent since onset of use.

stats.line: Getting hooked on cocaine peaks at age 23–25. Most who get hooked do so within 3 years of first use.
stats.mirror: Men in their early-to-mid twenties using a bit more each year.

basis.design: national survey (National Comorbidity Survey), survival analysis
basis.measured: age at first use, and age when people first met dependence criteria

stats.caveat: Older data. 'Most' means most of those who became dependent, not most users. Within 10 years, 15–16% of users had become dependent.

ref.cite: Wagner FA, Anthony JC (2002). From first drug use to drug dependence; developmental periods of risk for dependence upon marijuana, cocaine, and alcohol. Neuropsychopharmacology.
ref.quote: Peak values for cocaine dependence were found at age 23-25. ... Most of the observed cases of cocaine dependence met criteria for dependence within three years after initial cocaine use.

stats.line: 68% of men in cocaine rehab had had scary, short bursts of paranoia while using. It got worse and came faster over time.
stats.mirror: Guys who check the window or the door after a few lines.

basis.who: cocaine-dependent men entering a 28-day rehab program, one after another
basis.measured: whether they had had very distressing, short-lived paranoid states while using cocaine

stats.caveat: Small, older study of dependent men in rehab; lighter users likely have it less. The paranoia passed after use; it was not lasting illness.

ref.cite: Satel SL, Southwick SM, Gawin FH (1991). Clinical features of cocaine-induced paranoia. American Journal of Psychiatry.
ref.quote: Thirty-four (68%) of the 50 men reported highly distressing transient paranoid states in the context of cocaine use.

stats.line: In people off cocaine up to 12 weeks, 46 studies found moderately worse scores in 8 areas of thinking, including attention and memory.
stats.mirror: Men who forget things at work and act before thinking.

basis.who: people with cocaine abuse or dependence vs. healthy comparison groups
basis.measured: test scores in 11 areas of thinking, split by how long people had been off cocaine

stats.caveat: Group averages, not a prediction for you. The gaps were small in people off 20 weeks or more.

ref.cite: Potvin S, Stavro K, Rizkallah E, et al. (2014). Cocaine and cognition: a systematic quantitative review. Journal of Addiction Medicine.
ref.quote: Findings revealed moderate impairment across 8 cognitive domains during intermediate abstinence. The most impaired domains were attention, impulsivity, verbal learning/memory, and working memory.

stats.line: Of men treated for cocaine addiction in 1988–89, 52% had been cocaine-free for 5 years or more when checked 12 years later.
stats.mirror: Anyone who thinks cocaine addiction is a life sentence.

basis.who: men (veterans) admitted to treatment for cocaine dependence in 1988–1989
basis.measured: whether they had used no cocaine for at least 5 years at the 12-year interview

stats.caveat: Only men who were found and interviewed. All had been in treatment. It does not say how many attempts it took.

ref.cite: Herbeck DM, Hser YI, Lu AT, et al. (2006). A 12-year follow-up study of psychiatric symptomatology among cocaine-dependent men. Addictive Behaviors.
ref.quote: Of the 266 study participants interviewed at the 12-year follow-up, 138 (52%) had been cocaine abstinent for 5 years or more.

stats.line: Adding counselling or a reward program made people about twice as likely to be fully clean at the end of treatment.
stats.mirror: Men deciding whether to get help or go it alone.

basis.measured: continuous abstinence at the end of treatment, compared with no added treatment

stats.caveat: Low-quality evidence. At the longest follow-up the gain was no longer clear. Many comparison groups still got some care.

ref.cite: Minozzi S, Saulle R, De Crescenzo F, Amato L (2016). Psychosocial interventions for psychostimulant misuse. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: increased continuous abstinence at the end of treatment (RR: 2.14, 95% CI 1.27 to -3.59, 8 studies, 1241 participants, low quality evidence)

stats.line: Felt craving drops steadily after quitting, but the brain reacts most to cocaine cues at 1 to 6 months off.
stats.mirror: Men a few months clean who feel safe and drop their guard.

basis.design: lab study comparing groups off cocaine for different lengths of time
basis.who: adults addicted to cocaine, off for 2 days, 1 week, 1 month, 6 months or 1 year
basis.measured: brain-wave (EEG) response to cocaine pictures, and self-rated craving

stats.caveat: Different people at each time point, not the same people followed. A brain reaction is not a relapse; relapse was not measured.

ref.cite: Parvaz MA, Moeller SJ, Goldstein RZ (2016). Incubation of cue-induced craving in adults addicted to cocaine measured by electroencephalography. JAMA Psychiatry.
ref.quote: the mean (SD) late positive potential amplitudes showed a parabolic trajectory that was higher at 1 (1.26 [1.36] µV) and 6 (1.17 [1.19] µV) months of abstinence

stats.line: Rewards for clean urine tests, plus help building a life without cocaine, gave 7.6× the odds of being clean at 12 weeks.
stats.mirror: Men who respond to rewards and structure more than to willpower talks.

basis.who: adults with cocaine and/or amphetamine addiction
basis.where: several countries (not listed in the abstract)
basis.measured: share clean on urine tests, compared with usual care

stats.caveat: Odds, not chance. The range is wide (2.0 to 28.4) and falls to 3.1× at the longest follow-up. Includes amphetamine trials.

ref.cite: De Crescenzo F, Ciabattini M, D'Alò GL, et al. (2018). Comparative efficacy and acceptability of psychosocial interventions for individuals with cocaine and amphetamine addiction: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. PLoS Medicine.
ref.quote: and also at 12 weeks (OR 7.60, 95% CI 2.03-28.37, P = 0.002) and at longest follow-up (OR 3.08, 95% CI 1.33-7.17, P = 0.008)

stats.line: Two weeks off cocaine, people said they slept well, but sleep tests showed their sleep was at its worst.
stats.mirror: Men two weeks clean who feel fine but are tired and slow.

basis.measured: sleep by overnight brain-wave recording vs. their own ratings, plus alertness and learning

stats.caveat: Only 12 people in a lab. It shows sleep can feel better than it is. Alertness and learning also dipped then.

ref.cite: Morgan PT, Pace-Schott EF, Sahul ZH, et al. (2006). Sleep, sleep-dependent procedural learning and vigilance in chronic cocaine users: evidence for occult insomnia. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.
ref.quote: total sleep time and sleep latency were at their worst by 14-17 days of abstinence while self-reported sleep was at its best.

stats.line: Twelve years after treatment, men who stayed off cocaine had fewer mental-health symptoms than men still using, on 4 of 5 measures.
stats.mirror: Men who wonder if the anxiety and low mood will ever lift.

basis.who: men (veterans) admitted to treatment for cocaine dependence in 1988–1989
basis.measured: a 58-item checklist of mental-health symptoms at intake and at 1, 2 and 12 years

stats.caveat: Both groups improved in the first year. A link: men who stayed off may have differed from the start. Men only.

ref.cite: Herbeck DM, Hser YI, Lu AT, et al. (2006). A 12-year follow-up study of psychiatric symptomatology among cocaine-dependent men. Addictive Behaviors.
ref.quote: By 12-year follow-up, the abstinent group reported significantly lower SCL scores than the non-abstinent group on 4 of the 5 symptom measures.

stats.line: Users who stopped cocaine reached the same thinking scores as non-users within a year. Those who cut use by 72% improved a little.
stats.mirror: Men worried cocaine left them permanently slower.

basis.design: cohort followed 1 year (Zurich Cocaine Cognition Study)
basis.who: cocaine users and people who never used stimulants
basis.n: 57 users (19 used more, 19 less, 19 the same) and 48 controls
basis.measured: 13 test scores (attention, working memory, memory, planning) at the start and after 1 year; use checked with hair tests

stats.caveat: Small groups of mostly moderate users. People who started young recovered working memory less well.

ref.cite: Vonmoos M, Hulka LM, Preller KH, et al. (2014). Cognitive impairment in cocaine users is drug-induced but partially reversible: evidence from a longitudinal study. Neuropsychopharmacology.
ref.quote: cognitive impairment might be partially cocaine-induced but also reversible within 1 year, at least after moderate exposure.

stats.line: Thinking problems tend to stay through the first months off cocaine, then may fade after about 5 months clean.
stats.mirror: Men 2–3 months clean who still feel foggy.

basis.who: people with cocaine abuse or dependence vs. healthy comparison groups
basis.measured: test scores by time off: still testing positive, up to 12 weeks, 20 weeks or more

stats.caveat: 'May' is the authors' word: fewer studies looked at long abstinence. Group averages, not a promise for you.

ref.cite: Potvin S, Stavro K, Rizkallah E, et al. (2014). Cocaine and cognition: a systematic quantitative review. Journal of Addiction Medicine.
ref.quote: Cognitive dysfunctions remain stable during the first months of abstinence and may abate after 5 months of sobriety.

stats.line: In men who stopped cocaine, low mood and craving were worst on the first day and eased steadily over 28 days.
stats.mirror: Men in their first days off who feel low.

basis.who: male cocaine addicts, mostly injecting, living in a research unit, vs. non-addicted men
basis.where: USA (National Institute on Drug Abuse unit, Maryland)
basis.measured: mood, craving and sleep ratings over 28 days

stats.caveat: Tiny, old study of mostly injecting users, with no cocaine around. Their mood was still worse than the controls'.

ref.cite: Weddington WW, Brown BS, Haertzen CA, et al. (1990). Changes in mood, craving, and sleep during short-term abstinence reported by male cocaine addicts. Archives of General Psychiatry.
ref.quote: Addicts' mood-distress scores and craving for cocaine were greatest at admission and decreased gradually and steadily during the 28-day study.

rejected.claim: 18–25× higher risk of sudden death when cocaine is mixed with alcohol (cocaethylene; van Amsterdam 2024).
rejected.why: A death statistic. The owner does not want those, so it was not given a basis.

rejected.claim: European cocaine use, price per gram, and years from first use to first treatment (EUDA European Drug Report 2025).
rejected.why: EUDA's site returned 403 (Cloudflare) to every fetch, so nothing could be verified.

rejected.claim: 25 million people used cocaine worldwide in 2023 (UNODC World Drug Report 2025).
rejected.why: Only the UNODC press release could be fetched; the rules exclude press-release-only numbers.

rejected.claim: About 1 in 6 past-year cocaine users has cocaine use disorder (NSDUH).
rejected.why: No fetched source states this share. It could be worked out from 0.37% and 2.14% (Mustaquim 2021), but the rules forbid derived numbers. SAMHSA's own reports were blocked (403).

rejected.claim: Share who relapse in the first 1–3 months after cocaine treatment.
rejected.why: No fetched abstract gave a clear percentage (Sinha 2006 reports time to relapse, but no rates). Parvaz 2016's 1–6 month window is used instead.

rejected.claim: How many quit attempts cocaine users usually make.
Cocaine remission about 14% per year, or 5% (Calabria 2010 review).
rejected.why: Only 4 cocaine studies, mixed definitions, and the abstract does not clearly say per year. Too unclear to show.

rejected.claim: Only 24.6% of Americans with a lifetime drug use disorder ever got treatment (Grant 2016, NESARC-III).
rejected.why: Verified, but covers all drugs, not cocaine alone. Left out.

rejected.claim: Money: what a regular user spends per year.
rejected.why: No official per-user spending figure found; price data (EUDA) was blocked. Not computed.
Only a 102-man mixed-drug clinic sample (32.3% had ED, Clemente 2017), not cocaine-specific. Not used.

rejected.claim: Prefrontal grey matter grew back after 6 months of no or less use (Parvaz 2017).
rejected.why: Verified, left out to stay at 14 new stats: only 19 people.
